274259.deck: Wolf wins a television contest, then has to become a real hero.

overview.text: Wolf enters a television contest for money and fame. Winning sends him into a parallel world, where Tina, the Witch of Dimensions, asks him to stop Dr. J. When she is kidnapped, rescuing her becomes his only way home. The fighting uses polygonal characters but largely follows a left-and-right path; the camera changes angle as Wolf moves through the stages.

development.text: Com2uS brought an existing phone game to Zeebo. The South Korean BREW release dates to September 2006, almost three years before the Brazilian console edition.

release.text: Action Hero 3D joined the Brazilian launch lineup on 25 May 2009. At 990 Z-Credits, it was the cheapest game in ZeeboNet when the reproduced ZeeboBrasil review assessed it. The reviewer found the camera could make distances hard to judge but considered the simple fighting accessible, particularly for younger players.

280386.deck: Alice solves puzzles with four companions and a second Wonderland behind the mirrors.

overview.text: Alice can cross between Wonderland and its mirror world. The White Rabbit alters time, the Cheshire Cat reveals hidden objects, the March Hare moves them, and the Mad Hatter sends them between worlds. Reaching the next area means working out whose ability to use and where.

development.text: Disney Interactive Studios Beijing made the original mobile game; Zeebo Interactive Studios adapted it for the console. The credits separate the two teams. Danny Caldas led development and also worked on art, alongside artists Luiz Gustavo Marquetti and Marcelo Silva. Olímpio MacLouly and Thomas Gomes are named as developers, Hugo Faria as producer, Denis Koishi as musician and Cacau Pastorello as QA lead.

release.text: Disney Mobile announced the Zeebo partnership on 1 September 2010. Alice reached the Brazilian service on 9 November, when the official blog invited owners to download it that afternoon. The launch description tied the puzzles to Tim Burton’s film and highlighted hidden objects collected in Alice’s journal.

276151.deck: Ski and snowboard down mountain courses, with jumps along the way.

overview.text: Alpine Racer offers downhill skiing and snowboarding. Players choose a character, race through snowy courses and perform aerial tricks.

development.text: This Alpine Racer came from Namco’s mobile lineup. Its BREW edition appeared in 2008, followed by iPhone and Zeebo versions in 2009. Namco Bandai Games is credited as developer, with Namco Networks publishing and Tectoy distributing the Zeebo release.

This release family was already moving between mobile platforms before Zeebo launched. In February 2009, Stuart Dredge saw Apple demonstrate Namco’s iPhone version, with both skiing and snowboarding. His preview explicitly warned that its illustration came from the earlier handset game. The Zeebo release followed in May, using a television and Z-Pad rather than the iPhone’s touch-and-tilt setup.

release.text: Alpine Racer was available at the Brazilian console launch on 25 May 2009.

280214.deck: Propeller aircraft fight over a fictional Second World War.

overview.text: Armageddon Squadron is an arcade flight game. Its missions send the player against air and ground targets in a fictional Second World War setting.
The campaign contains 12 missions, sending aircraft against land, sea and air targets with machine guns, bombs, rockets and torpedoes. An arcade mode lets players set up their own challenges.

development.text: Polarbit developed the game and announced a Zeebo version in April 2010.

The agreement formed part of Polarbit’s move from handheld devices into home set-top systems. Founder Mitri Bautista-Wiberg said the Zeebo deal could reach customers the studio normally could not. Armageddon Squadron and Iron Sight shipped first; the two racing games followed later.

release.text: The Zeebo release reached Brazil in September 2010, distributed by Zeebo Brasil.

Ahtrun’s 5 October 2010 review was disappointed by the result. The campaign and custom missions supplied content, but the reviewer criticised stretched-looking graphics, static water and sky, weak engine sounds and the lack of music during missions. No multiplayer mode was available.

277083.deck: Rotate four gems at a time to build matches.

overview.text: Bejeweled Twist changes the usual gem swap into a rotation. Turning a group of coloured stones lines up matches and can set off further combinations.
The Classic mode introduces locked gems and counters that must be cleared before they expire. Zen offers a gentler alternative. Larger matches create special gems that can clear more of the board.

development.text: The Zeebo credits distinguish the original design by Brian Fiete, Jason Kapalka and Kurt Pfeifer from the later engineering and production teams. Vincent McCreith is credited for music on this edition.

release.text: Bejeweled Twist reached Brazil on 29 September 2009, becoming PopCap’s first Zeebo game.

STX’s April 2010 review liked the music and puzzle challenge, but described unreliable D-pad input. His workaround was to use the right analogue stick, start Bejeweled first after powering on and avoid long pauses. A reader, Ahtrun, objected that accepting a workaround did not make the controls satisfactory:

274214.deck: Crash and his rivals race karts and attack each other with collected items.

overview.text: Crash, Coco, Cortex and their rivals race through three cups of four courses. Drifting helps with tight corners, jumps clear obstacles, and collected weapons interrupt the other racers. Quick Race gets straight to a starting grid; the main menu also offers a tutorial, story events and time trials.
The courses move through different environments, including the underwater and space settings advertised in the Zeebo guide. Shortcuts and speed strips offer ways to regain a place after an attack.

development.text: Tectoy Digital adapted Polarbit’s iPhone game for Zeebo. Producer Tiago Tex Pine dates the work to 2008–2009 and recalls a small programming group working for a couple of months. The C/C++ game used Polarbit’s engine; the adaptation also required interface assets and new screens for the console.

The work changed how the game was played. Touch-screen interactions had to be retuned for a physical controller, and the port supported the Boomerang motion accessory. Pine describes reviewing and testing the build in Scrum cycles, managing its budget and staffing, and adding Brazilian Portuguese localisation. His project summary also records Spanish localisation.
The published credits name Tiago Tex Pine and Hugo Faria in production, and Vitor Picanço do Amaral, Tiago Monteiro Fernandes, Leonardo Loures Lopes and Bruno Evangelista in programming.

release.text: Crash was one of the games used to demonstrate Zeebo before release. Reviewing the console edition in March 2010, Daniel (Chrome) noted its colourful scenery and busy races, but also slowdown when many racers and items filled the screen. He found that an earlier demonstration’s delayed music start had been fixed in the finished version.

The lack of split-screen racing disappointed the reviewer. Boomerang support produced a different response: in a later comment beneath the review, Daniel said motion control made the game more exciting than using the Z-Pad.

280173.deck: Six card games with Mickey, Minnie, Donald, Daisy and Goofy.

overview.text: Disney All Star Cards brings together six card games. Each table has one human player and three computer opponents. Pixie dust can buy cards and gallery artwork, or be spent on a game-specific cheat.

release.text: Disney Mobile and Zeebo announced their partnership on 1 September 2010, targeting Disney All Star Cards for 21 September. Alice in Wonderland and Jelly Car 2 were also named in the proposed lineup, alongside two unnamed titles. The deal was meant to bring Disney’s mobile catalog into Brazilian and Mexican living rooms.

274754.deck: Billy and Jimmy Lee return in a six-mission remake.

overview.text: Billy and Jimmy Lee set out to rescue Marian from Machine Gun Willy’s gang. The Zeebo remake expands the arcade game from four missions to six, with three new locations. Weapons dropped by enemies can be picked up and used, and oil drums can be thrown or kicked.
Finishing the game opens up more playable fighters. The extra battle mode lets players return as the enemies, with eighteen unlockable characters and their own sets of moves.

The controller supports both single-button moves and some combined-button commands. Weapons can be dropped deliberately, while dashing and launch attacks can be linked into mid-air combinations. Rockman’s detailed Zeebo review made those juggling attacks a particular attraction.

development.text: Brizo Interactive and Million are credited on this remake. Its Zeebo staff include main planner Hiroto Ikuta, main programmer Seiji Ando, graphic artists Hiroto Kittaka and Yuji Watanabe, and composer Hideki Asanaka. Souta Ichino led the project, with Ryosuke Jinno as sub-producer.
Brizo later made an iPhone Double Dragon. In an April 2011 interview, Jinno described that release as the studio’s third Double Dragon project, following its earlier mobile and Zeebo work.

release.text: Access itself became part of the game’s history. Double Dragon Dojo contributor Rockman described buying a Brazilian Zeebo through an auction site, using Google Translate, and finding one with Double Dragon already installed. He praised its fighting options, enemy roster and unlockable Extra mode.

A review reproduced at Zeebo Club in March 2010 was more reserved about the fighting. It praised the redrawn sprites but described attack sequences that could not be cancelled, leaving a fighter exposed when punches missed. The writer considered the result enjoyable, with less fluid combat than it could have had.

notes.text: Ryosuke Jinno’s 2011 interview concerns the later iPhone remake. Its fifteen-person team and ten-month schedule must not be assigned to the Zeebo production.

274803.deck: Football with friendly matches, challenges, seasons and tournaments.

overview.text: FIFA 09 on Zeebo offers four modes: a friendly match for one or two players, ten set challenges, a full season in one of eleven leagues, and a choice of ten tournaments. Players can change their lineup and roles, while a stamina meter limits continuous running.

development.text: The credits retain Gamelion’s team, led by Krzysztof Jędruczyk, with producers Hubert Borowy and Sebastian Szczygieł. The Brazilian adaptation team included producer Hugo Faria; programmers Edgar Vilela Gadbem, Henrique Mendes and Leonardo Loures Lopes; artists Carina Cheng, Seigi Sato and Suellen Salgado; and musician Denis Koishi.
John Rizzo described FIFA as a hybrid: part of the game came from mobile content, while the voiceovers came from PC.

That included Portuguese commentary by Nivaldo Prieto. The reproduced ZeeboBrasil review also identified Curumin’s recording “Magrela Fever” in the menus. The commentary and licensed music brought familiar elements from the larger FIFA releases into a much smaller game.

release.text: FIFA 09 was installed on the first Brazilian retail consoles. Claudio Prandoni’s June 2009 UOL report criticised its slow response and rudimentary presentation while noting that the promised Portuguese commentary was present.

The ZeeboBrasil review preserved by Zeebo Club was similarly mixed: licensed teams, Brazilian clubs and several competition modes were welcome, but player movement and defensive behaviour felt crude. The writer specifically noted that tackling was semi-automatic, with no dedicated tackle button.

notes.text: The Polish Gamelion credits and Brazilian adaptation credits are retained as separate teams. MobyGames’ full credit URL returned 403; its indexed game page and BDJogos’ Brazilian roll were available.

277380.deck: A Terran mercenary takes contracts in the war against the Vossk.

overview.text: A Terran mercenary takes combat, capture and escort contracts during the war against the Vossk. After the opening missions, the map opens up: the player can choose destinations and jobs, move between planets and space stations, and earn money towards a better ship.

Stations with trading facilities sell ships, weapons and shields. Cargo recovered during missions, including medicines and electronics, can be sold to finance the next upgrade. Difficulty, aiming, inverted controls and language settings are adjustable; the Zeebo edition offers English, Spanish and Portuguese.

development.text: Galaxy on Fire began on Java phones, including the Sony Ericsson K700 with its 176 × 220 display. Fishlabs already knew Qualcomm’s Mike Yuen through its BREW games. Michael Schade contacted him before GDC 2009, and the resulting meeting led to Fishlabs’ first console release.
Fishlabs adapted Galaxy on Fire using its ABYSS engine. Michael Schade explained which versions supplied the code and artwork:
The first Zeebo builds ran too slowly. The team reduced assets and reorganised textures, eventually reaching roughly four times its initial frame rate.
Television output introduced other constraints. Strong colours could bleed and fine horizontal lines could flicker; the absence of OpenAL required changes to the sound engine.

Schade said the analogue controller was the adaptation’s most important difference from the phone editions. Reaching a first playable version was quick with the existing ABYSS engine and C code; getting the performance and television output right took further work.

release.text: The September 2009 announcement highlighted survival play, revised AI and interface work, and updated sound and music. These were advertised changes accompanying the move from phones to the television.

Writing for Zeebo Club in October, gui welcomed the larger adventure and the Z-Pad controls, but missed Boomerang support. The review recommended the game while acknowledging that long sessions could become tiring; readers beneath it also disagreed about how quickly its mission loop became repetitive.

278200.deck: Drive a tank through waves of aircraft, vehicles and heavier weapons.

overview.text: Heavy Weapon is a side-scrolling tank shooter with enemies attacking from land, sea and air. Equipment upgrades are available between stages.

The two analogue sticks have different jobs: the left moves the tank and the right aims its gun. The campaign revisits nine areas before a nineteenth, final stage, increasing the difficulty as the player returns through them.

development.text: Vega Mobile made the Zeebo version from an existing mobile adaptation. The credits name Wayne Imlach, René Laurent, Eric Thommerot and Philip Plunkett on that earlier work, with Viktorya Hollings as executive producer of the Zeebo edition.

release.text: Heavy Weapon had launched in Brazil and Mexico by PopCap’s March 2010 Zeebo announcement.

J.Vila’s review described a game that arrived without the expectations surrounding Resident Evil 4 and proved more enjoyable than its modest presentation suggested. The reviewer criticised repetitive aircraft designs and music but praised the rising difficulty and effective controls, awarding 7/10.

280221.deck: Turn-based robot battles between the Corporation and the Rebellion.

overview.text: Iron Sight gives each side time to move and aim before firing. Players fight for the Corporation or the Rebellion, using missiles and items such as teleporters. Holding the fire button increases a shot’s range; releasing it launches the weapon.
The Zeebo campaign contains eight levels with different terrain and enemy positions. A multiplayer mode offers another way to play.

development.text: The Zeebo credits name Deion Mobile as the developer and list five authors: Tomek Wagner, Raymond Leung, Bartek Tajer, Vyach Imalkovski and Justin Wasack.
Polarbit’s Zeebo agreement covered four titles, with Iron Sight and Armageddon Squadron forming the first wave. By 30 September 2010 both were available in Brazil and Mexico.

release.text: Polarbit brought Iron Sight to Zeebo. It was available in Brazil and Mexico by the end of September 2010.

STX’s November 2010 review found responsive movement but troublesome aiming: the player could adjust trajectory and force, yet the fixed view made depth difficult to judge. The review also noted that music heard in the menu disappeared during battle. Despite those complaints, its campaign and multiplayer could still hold the attention of a player who liked turn-based combat.

276121.deck: Build a racing crew and take on rival teams across the city.

overview.text: The crew house is the hub for choosing cars, checking the city map and managing teammates. Events include taking down rival cars and escaping an enemy crew’s territory before time runs out.

development.text: Tectoy Digital made the Zeebo version of Own the City, sold here as Domine a Cidade. Hugo Faria produced it, Bruno Evangelista led programming and Seigi Sato led art. The larger adaptation team included programmers Gustavo Galembeck and Tiago Monteiro Fernandes, with music by Denis Koishi.

The credit roll separates the earlier game’s team from a section headed “Zeebo Version Developed by Tectoy Digital”. That Brazilian team also included acting producer André Nogueira, QA lead Cacau Pastorello and artists Carina Cheng, Luiz Gustavo Marquetti, Marcelo Silva, Pedro Hamaya, Suellen Salgado and Wilson Hideki Akamine.

release.text: Need for Speed was one of three games embedded in the original Brazilian retail console, alongside FIFA 09 and Treino Cerebral.

The ZeeboBrasil review reproduced by Zeebo Club liked the Portuguese dialogue, translated interface and substantial soundtrack. It was much less forgiving of the races: slow acceleration, a weak sense of speed, sparse traffic and dark, repetitive scenery. The review awarded 4.5/10. Reader Saulo Albert pushed back against the verdict, adding that the game had been included free:

quotes.text: Apesar de todas as críticas o considero um bom jogo.
quotes.original_text: Apesar de todas as críticas o considero um bom jogo.
quotes.speaker: Saulo Albert, player
quotes.attribution: Comment on the Zeebo Club review, 21 April 2010
quotes.translation: English translation by the archive: “Despite all the criticism, I consider it a good game.”

278962.deck: Fire a ball into the board and clear every orange peg.

overview.text: Peggle turns each shot into a bouncing path through a field of pegs. Its ten masters supply different powers for clearing the orange targets.

development.text: Vega Mobile handled the Zeebo conversion. Its credit roll preserves Brian Rothstein and Sukhbir Sidhu’s original concept separately from the production, engineering and art roles, then explicitly identifies Vega as the console-version studio. This was part of the same PopCap adaptation work that brought Heavy Weapon to Zeebo.

release.text: Peggle was available on Zeebo by 9 March 2010. PopCap’s announcement lists 55 main levels, ten unlockable masters, Quick Play, Duel, and a further 55 Challenge levels.

STX’s May 2010 review found a cheerful game with more tactical appeal than its appearance initially suggested. Both the D-pad and analogue stick could aim, although the analogue movement sometimes became excessively fast. Large chains of hits could also cause slowdown. The turn-taking Duel mode was a particular attraction for local play.

quotes.attribution: Zeebo Club review, 30 May 2010

280238.deck: Race powerboats around buoys and unlock new islands.

overview.text: Powerboat Challenge offers four pilots with boats that have different handling traits. A tutorial explains steering and passing the buoys. Completing enough events opens the next island, with conventional races and elimination events among the challenges.

Money earned from events buys improvements for the boat, while medals unlock island championships. Passing close to the correct side of a buoy replenishes turbo; missing a gate costs speed and can eventually disqualify the racer.

development.text: Fishlabs developed the game. The Zeebo credits name Lars Berger and Stefan Görlich as lead developers, Henning Lubahn for 3D and level design, and Gero Goerlich for music and sound effects. Jörg Thomaschewski produced it.

The Zeebo edition supported the Boomerang as well as the Z-Pad. STX found that motion-control play used automatic acceleration, with the Boomerang’s directional buttons handling braking and turbo. The Z-Pad offered more precise control, while the Boomerang changed the feel of steering.

release.text: Powerboat Challenge launched on 12 October 2010, Brazilian Children’s Day. The official post encouraged players to earn money and customise their boats.

STX’s November review praised the environments and Boomerang support, but found occasional stutters and a conspicuous lack of engine noise. The race music was a rock-and-drum-and-bass mixture rather than an engine soundtrack. Local multiplayer was absent.

quotes.text: jogar com o Z-pad é muito mais preciso
quotes.original_text: jogar com o Z-pad é muito mais preciso
quotes.speaker: STX
quotes.attribution: Zeebo Club review, 5 November 2010
quotes.translation: English translation by the archive: “Playing with the Z-pad is much more precise.”

276154.deck: Tommy searches for Jenny through an alien spacecraft, with weapons and Spirit Walk.

overview.text: Prey Evil belongs to the mobile retelling of Prey. Tommy searches for his missing girlfriend Jenny, fighting with a wrench, rifle and organic grenades. The adventure is divided into chapters and discrete levels. Spirit Walk lets him leave his body to solve obstacles; defeat can send him into a spirit realm to recover health and power.

development.text: The Zeebo credits name Seth A. Robinson as lead programmer, Andreas Vasen as producer and Scott Miller as executive producer. Les Pardew and Weston Tracy are credited for art.

Seth A. Robinson had already programmed MachineWorks’ BREW games, including Duke Nukem Mobile 3D and Rocky Balboa 3D. His project history lists Prey Evil for Zeebo and Prey Invasion for iPhone as separate 2009 assignments.
Before launch, John Rizzo estimated that the Zeebo adaptation was taking roughly seven months.

QSound’s June 2009 financial statement confirms that Prey Evil licensed its Ripp3D graphics engine. The free-download arrangement paid QSound a royalty for every console sold in Brazil; the company also discussed additional games as future plans.

release.text: In June 2009, QSound said Zeebo purchasers were entitled to download Prey Evil free of charge.
Claudio Prandoni’s launch report judged Prey’s movement and actions unusually responsive among the first Zeebo games. He also found some levels little more than straight corridors with a few enemies.

274802.deck: Fight through military bases, castles and dungeons filled with monsters.

overview.text: Quake sends the player through military bases, medieval castles and lava-filled dungeons in search of four runes. Knights, ogres and other creatures stand in the way. Finding keys and hidden supplies is as much a part of reaching the exit as surviving the next fight.

development.text: Quake came from id Software’s PC game. Before Zeebo launched, CEO John Rizzo explained how long that conversion had taken:
The Zeebo adaptation retains credits for the original id Software team alongside a separate console production and programming group.

Rafael Nanya and Heriberto Martinez Manrique are credited as the Zeebo chief engineers. The port’s programmers include Cesar Dantas de Castro, Ricardo Destro, Rafael Dazcal, Ademir José Barba and Mauricio Antonio Guerta. André Penha and Reinaldo Normand served as executive producers.

release.text: Claudio Prandoni tested a retail Zeebo for UOL in June 2009. Quake was one of the machine’s stronger demonstrations: he found it smooth and noted that the earlier English build had been localised into Portuguese.

A Zeebo Blog statement dated 17 June 2010, reproduced in a contemporary forum post, confirmed that Quake and Quake II had been permanently removed from the store. Existing downloads would keep working if owners did not delete them. New buyers would instead receive Extreme Rolimã and Jetboard.

quotes.text: Quake, which was strictly a port from the PC, took about six months.
quotes.speaker: John Rizzo, Zeebo CEO
quotes.attribution: Interview with Brandon Sheffield, Gamasutra, 9 January 2009

quotes.text: rodando de forma suave, sem engasgar
quotes.speaker: Claudio Prandoni
quotes.attribution: UOL Jogos, 9 June 2009
quotes.translation: English translation by the archive: “running smoothly, without stuttering.”

276153.deck: A surviving soldier takes the fight to the Strogg homeworld.

overview.text: After the Strogg attack Earth, humanity launches an assault on their homeworld. The operation fails, leaving a surviving soldier to fight through the aliens’ military installations and disable their war machine. Quake II builds its first-person shooting around this campaign through enemy territory.

development.text: Adapting Quake II meant bringing the original C game into an ARM/BREW environment. Producer Tiago Tex Pine recalls that the PC game’s memory-allocation approach did not fit the console’s operating system. Performance and rendering needed substantial attention rather than a straightforward recompile.

Pine led a seven-person group of developers and QA staff. He tested and tuned the controls and camera for the Zeebo hardware, managed the project, and supplied some voices himself. The work included Portuguese and Spanish text and voice localisation.

The adaptation’s credits identify the programmers and the Portuguese voice cast separately from id Software’s original team. Suzana Bueno voices the computers and Bruno Santos the radio; members of the programming team also voiced prisoners.

release.text: Quake II’s early availability was uneven. UOL could not test it in June 2009 because, according to Tectoy’s press office, problems had caused its removal from the download servers.

By March 2010, Daniel (Chrome) could review the game for Zeebo Club. He praised the Portuguese voice work and the full sequence of PC levels, while noting reduced lighting, missing introductory video and no multiplayer. He also recorded reports of downloads appearing on some consoles but not others, and crashes when new areas loaded.

The console offered two control presets. Casual added automatic aiming; Expert used one analogue stick to move and the other to look. Aim sensitivity could be adjusted. Daniel found the Z-Pad’s small sticks took practice, but welcomed hearing Brazilian Portuguese radio chatter during the opening mission.
Quake II was later removed from sale alongside Quake. The company’s June 2010 statement said existing downloaded copies could still be played, provided they had not been deleted.

quotes.text: uma boa dublagem, diga-se
quotes.speaker: Daniel (Chrome)
quotes.attribution: Zeebo Club review, 29 March 2010; discussing the Portuguese radio voices
quotes.translation: English translation by the archive: “good voice acting, at that.”

280602.deck: An arcade street racer from Polarbit’s Zeebo lineup.

overview.text: Raging Thunder 2 is a street racer built around buying and upgrading cars. Its routes pass through beaches, snowy mountains, temple ruins and the Great Wall. Pixelbite’s portfolio describes five single-player modes, including Survival and Time Attack.

development.text: Pixelbite includes the game in its own portfolio, and the Zeebo release record credits Pixelbite as developer with Polarbit publishing. It formed part of Polarbit’s four-game agreement for the console, announced in April 2010. The first two games arrived in September; the racing games were held for the holiday lineup.

release.text: The Zeebo edition was released on 7 December 2010, completing Polarbit’s announced holiday lineup after the September launches of Armageddon Squadron and Iron Sight.

notes.text: Pixelbite’s current portfolio advertises online and cross-platform multiplayer for the broader mobile release. Those features have not been independently established for this preserved Zeebo package.

studio_roles.name: Pixelbite
studio_roles.role: Developer credited by GameFAQs; title appears in studio portfolio

278282.deck: Rally stages on asphalt, loose stones, sand and snow.

overview.text: Rally Master Pro offers four modes across courses with different surfaces. The Zeebo guide lists asphalt, stones, sand and snow.

Career opens the other modes as the player progresses. Adrenaline allows a choice of course and weather, and repair minigames interrupt the racing to fix vehicle damage. The Zeebo review praised changes in handling between surfaces and weather conditions.

development.text: Fishlabs developed and published the game. It began on Java phones in 2008, then reached Zeebo in Brazil in December 2009, with Tectoy handling distribution.

Before the console conversion, Fishlabs used the original phone game to test a different distribution model. In 2008, Michael Schade described releasing a free client through pirate sites and charging virtual credits to unlock more tracks. The company wanted to measure repeat play and demand without relying entirely on mobile-operator storefronts. That experiment concerned the phone edition, not ZeeboNet.

release.text: The Brazilian Zeebo release followed on 21 December 2009.

Ahtrun’s May 2010 review praised immediate controls, a steady frame rate and the repair minigames. The omissions were as noticeable: no multiplayer and only four car models, without player choice or customisation. Occasional sound faults and the difficulty of the highest setting also drew criticism.

quotes.text: Jogabilidade perfeita sem atraso nos controles
quotes.original_text: Jogabilidade perfeita sem atraso nos controles
quotes.speaker: Ahtrun
quotes.attribution: Zeebo Club review, 16 May 2010
quotes.translation: English translation by the archive: “Perfect gameplay with no delay in the controls.”

overview.text: Reckless Racing follows cars around off-road tracks from an overhead viewpoint. Pixelbite developed the game.

development.text: Reckless Racing was Pixelbite’s third game and its first project that was not work-for-hire. The studio had wanted to make an old-fashioned top-down racer with the detail and feel of a console game. Its portfolio credits Instant Remedy’s banjo soundtrack, alongside the bumps, slides and vehicle differences that made the racing distinctive.

It first appeared in the announced Zeebo lineup as Deliverace. By the November launch, the name had changed to Reckless Racing. Polarbit published the console version, while EA handled the contemporary iPhone and iPad release.

release.text: The official Zeebo blog announced availability on 3 November 2010, less than two weeks after the iPhone/iPad launch. It specifically told owners to use the wired controller. That instruction distinguishes the console controls from the tilt and touchscreen options promoted on phones.

276675.deck: Leon’s rescue mission retold in twelve chapters for the mobile and Zeebo editions.

overview.text: Resident Evil 4 Zeebo Edition breaks Leon’s rescue mission into twelve chapters, joined by cutscenes. It keeps the over-the-shoulder view and requires him to stop moving before he fires. The Merchant sells weapons and items using money earned during play.

Alongside its story, the console edition offers 24 Mercenary missions, unlocked two at a time through the twelve story missions, to earn money for equipment. Completing the story unlocks Professional mode; starting a new round retains money and weapons while resetting mission progress.

development.text: The Zeebo release credits Ideaworks3D as developer, Capcom as publisher and Tectoy as distributor. HI Corporation separately confirmed that this version used its MascotCapsule eruption technology.

The result is a chapter-based adaptation rather than the continuous console adventure. On-screen action prompts handle interactions such as placing ladders, kicking stunned enemies and evading boss attacks. The twelve-mission story and extra money-earning challenges change the rhythm of progression.

release.text: Resident Evil 4 and Ridge Racer appeared in the Brazilian catalog in August 2009. Cido Coelho’s contemporary report priced RE4 at 2490 Z-Credits, or R$24.90.

Mig64’s March 2010 review tried to assess the Zeebo release separately from the expectations attached to its name. The writer found the movement smooth and some boss fights demanding, but criticised the subdued sound, bright presentation and short or static missions. The conspicuous blue Ganados became part of the argument about the adaptation.

quotes.text: Port do celular? Sim, mas jogado no console, é o que importa.
quotes.original_text: Port do celular? Sim, mas jogado no console, é o que importa.

quotes.attribution: Zeebo Club review, 26 March 2010
quotes.translation: English translation by the archive: “Mobile port? Yes, but played on the console—that’s what matters.”

276152.deck: Namco’s mobile Ridge Racer, adapted for a television and controller.

overview.text: Ridge Racer offers car selection and three-dimensional road racing through city, mountain and coastal settings.

development.text: Ridge Racer’s route to Zeebo began with the mobile redesign released in 2005. Namco developed the game, with Namco Bandai publishing the console edition and Tectoy distributing it in Brazil.

release.text: Ridge Racer arrived alongside Resident Evil 4 in August 2009 at 1990 Z-Credits, equivalent to R$19.90. That price was a prominent part of the contemporary response.

Bruno Oz’s reaction, reproduced by GameVicio, described buying Ridge Racer and losing confidence in the console project. He thought parts of it looked worse than the phone version and objected to paying a home-console price for the conversion. This was one owner’s response, rather than a consensus score or an account from the development team.

quotes.text: Me sinto roubado em pagar R$20 por um jogo de celular capado.
quotes.original_text: Me sinto roubado em pagar R$20 por um jogo de celular capado.
quotes.speaker: Bruno Oz
quotes.attribution: Owner reaction, reproduced by GameVicio, 25 August 2009
quotes.translation: English translation by the archive: “I feel robbed paying R$20 for a cut-down mobile game.”

277455.deck: Regret searches for his past in an action RPG.

overview.text: Zenonia follows Regret through an adventure built around exploration, equipment and choices that affect his journey.

Players choose a paladin, warrior or assassin. Quests lead out from towns into real-time fights, while weight limits and a hunger/energy system require attention to supplies as well as equipment. Side quests offer more money and experience beyond the main route.

development.text: Zeebo was GAMEVIL’s first console release. Its November 2009 announcement emphasised localisation into Portuguese and Spanish, with the company treating Brazil and Mexico as a new audience for its existing RPG. The Mexican console launched on 4 November with Zenonia already installed, while Brazilian owners downloaded it.

release.text: The first months were troubled. In a December 2009 comment, a Zeebo Club reader complained that the game was full of bugs; another comment in April 2010 referred to a recall lasting months before owners could enjoy it again.

Lucas Mousinho’s review praised the 2D art and recommended the game to action-RPG players, while noting low apparent resolution, occasional slowdown and an automatic obstacle-avoidance behaviour he disliked. The controls used the D-pad, with separate buttons for attacks, menus, saving and the map.

notes.text: Portuguese Wikipedia links Tectoy’s official withdrawal notice (tecblog/?p=436) and return announcement (tecblog/?p=486). Both original URLs returned 404 and year-based Wayback lookups could not be retrieved in this pass. The precise withdrawal/refund/reissue chronology remains a follow-up rather than being reconstructed as verified fact.

quotes.translation: English translation by the archive: “the best game on Zeebo at the moment”

279712.deck: Fire coloured balls into moving chains and fight the island’s tiki bosses.

overview.text: Zuma’s Revenge returns to the ball-shooting puzzle game with hostile spirits and tiki bosses. Matching colours clears sections of the advancing chains.
The Zeebo edition has 60 levels and an additional challenge mode. Advancing chains leave little time to line up groups of three matching balls, and special shots can help stop the board from filling.

development.text: Vega Mobile ported PopCap’s game to Zeebo. Reflective Audio is credited for music.

release.text: The Brazilian Zeebo release followed in July 2010.

Ahtrun’s review appeared on 17 July 2010. It praised the long campaign, demanding stages and musical atmosphere, while finding the graphics comparatively lifeless and noting occasional sound interruptions and delayed controls. The review awarded 8/10. Its comments also show disagreement among owners: some welcomed the challenge while others wanted a wider variety of releases.

274804.deck: Twenty brain-training activities with daily progress tracking.

overview.text: Treino Cerebral is the Portuguese title of Gameloft’s Brain Challenge. Its 20 activities are divided into five categories, with daily exercises and charts that track the player’s results.

development.text: Brain Challenge already existed on click-wheel iPods in 2007. Gameloft’s announcement described twenty short exercises across memory, visual tasks, logic, mathematics and focus, with speed-and-accuracy scores and charts for daily progress. The Zeebo release brought that established brain-training format to a television and controller.
Gameloft’s Zeebo team was led by producer Alan Olvera and lead programmers Carlos Zarate and Favio Medrano. Enrique Nevarez handled 2D art, while Henri-Pierre Pellegrin worked on sound and music.

release.text: Treino Cerebral was one of three Portuguese-language games installed on the first Brazilian retail consoles when sales began on 25 May 2009.

studio_roles.name: Gameloft
studio_roles.role: Developer of Brain Challenge / Treino Cerebral

280634.deck: Six learning activities with Mônica, Magali, Cascão and their friends.

overview.text: Vamos Brincar nº 1 combines counting, colours, jigsaws, memory games and mazes. Anjinho needs particular balloons popped; Magali wants matching fruit found; Mônica helps Cascão cross a river and searches for Sansão. Marina’s painting activity also includes a free drawing tool.
There are three difficulty levels and 30 achievements. Players can import a Zeeboid to keep track of their achievements.

development.text: The game was made by Zeebo Interactive Studios in Campinas with Mauricio de Sousa Productions. Their November 2010 licensing announcement proposed nine educational and entertainment titles, including activity centres and games about maths and language.
Artist Alexandre Nacari identifies animation, assets and the graphical interface as his contributions. His portfolio names Flash and Photoshop as the tools he used for this 2010 project.

The planned partnership was broader than this one activity collection: four activity centres, four learning games and another Mônica game. The November announcement described a roughly 50-person Campinas studio working across programming, art, music, design and QA.

release.text: The Brazilian Zeebo game was released on 21 December 2010. Its published title is also recorded as Turma da Mônica em Vamos Brincar nº 1; this archive retains OpenZeebo’s “Vol. 1” label.
The partnership announcement initially targeted the first title for late November 2010 and a second for Christmas. The surviving release record places Vamos Brincar nº 1 in December.

notes.text: The nine-title licensing announcement describes planned work. It is not evidence that nine completed Mônica games reached Zeebo owners.

studio_roles.role: Licensed characters; animation and Portuguese voices

279036.deck: Toto and Willy’s platform adventure from the Mexican film Una Película de Huevos.

overview.text: Toto wants to become a chicken. Confi retells that journey in an alternative story based on Una Película de Huevos, with Toto and Willy as playable characters and a third character to unlock.
The game has 25 stages, five boss fights and ten unlockable competition stages. Two players can cooperate or race each other.

development.text: Fabrication Games developed the game, with Tommy Palm directing and Alexander Ekvall leading development and game design. David Telenius designed the levels, Henrik Pettersson led the art, and Oskar Rahm worked on 3D art and animation.
Huevocartoon’s team supplied the film characters and cutscenes. Jarpa Studio is credited for sound production.

The production brought together a Swedish game team and Mexican animation characters. The Zeebo credits separate Fabrication’s game design, levels and artwork from Huevocartoon’s direction, screenplay and animation. The lead artist, Henrik Pettersson, later joined Mojang to work on 2D art for Scrolls, a move reported by Frank Cifaldi in August 2011.

release.text: Un Juego de Huevos launched in Mexico on 19 April 2010. Brazil received it as Um Jogo de Ovos on 24 August 2010.

Zeebo promoted the Mexican launch for Children’s Day at 220 pesos. The 12 April announcement described the licence as a way to bring locally familiar characters to the console; its promised 19 April availability should be distinguished from the announcement’s own date.

Brazilian reviewer Ahtrun rated it 8.5/10 on 27 August 2010. He enjoyed the Spanish dialogue and the cooperative and competitive modes, while criticising repetitive backgrounds, monotonous music and a slight slide when Toto stopped moving. Multiplayer received his highest category score, 10/10.

274755.deck: The console’s main menu and game launcher.

overview.text: Z-Wheel starts when the console boots. It is the interface owners used to browse and open the games they had acquired.

The menu also displayed promotional slides and exposed services beyond launching games. Later preservation work documents how the final Brazilian software’s end-of-life setting disabled the main buttons except Play and Help when the 3G services ended.

development.text: O3 Labs’ later Z-Wheel Manager documents several launcher versions and supports conversion to the final Brazilian 1.0.727 release. Its author distinguishes configurable settings from executable patches, and describes replacing the now-unused browsing button with a local application manager. These are preservation modifications, not features of the original shop service.

274791.deck: A small system application recorded separately from Z-Wheel.

overview.text: Zeebo App appears as a separate entry in the console’s software inventory under ID 274791. Z-Wheel, which supplies the main menu and game launcher, has its own entry under ID 274755.

notes.text: The application’s exact user function and development credits have not been established for this record.

277495.deck: Web pages and curated channels on a television.

overview.text: The Portuguese game guide calls this service Z-Channels. It let owners browse the web through their television; OpenZeebo identifies the preserved application as Zeebo Channels (Opera Mini).

development.text: Opera Software adapted Opera Mini for Zeebo. The browser compressed web content before delivery over the mobile connection, while the console displayed pages on the television.

Opera described this as its first Opera Mini release for a home consumer-electronics device built on mobile technology. The stated aim was home web access for people otherwise using Internet cafés. Its compression reduced network traffic before pages reached the television; the companies’ speed and cost claims were marketing comparisons, not independent tests.

release.text: Opera and Zeebo announced Opera Mini for Mexico on 1 December 2009.

In Brazil, a 10 September 2010 official post said Z-Channels was already available. The application download was free; browsing time was sold in two-, four- or six-hour packages using Z-Credits, with two hours included on the first download.

studio_roles.scope: Opera Mini for Zeebo — Mexico announcement, 2009

279394.deck: Zeebo news, release announcements and promotions on the console.

overview.text: Zeebo Clube was a free application for following news from Zeebo without leaving the console. The company described release announcements, promotions and other information about the system.

release.text: Zeebo Brasil introduced the application on its official blog on 3 September 2010 and directed owners to install it from the console’s store. The post said availability for everyone would follow.

notes.text: The official post distinguished Zeebo Clube from ZeeboClub, an independent fan website with a similar name.

277727.deck: Off-road buggy racing with jumps and turbo boosts.

overview.text: Baja races small off-road cars across dirt tracks, caves and rough ground. Jumps interrupt the course, and collected fuel supplies a turbo boost.

development.text: Tiago Tex Pine led game design and production across the five Extreme games. He described the work involved:
The team grew to 23 while making the series during 2009, working towards a schedule of one finished game every two months.

Baja was already part of the studio’s public plans in February 2009, alongside wakeboard racing. At that stage the announcement described Extreme as a growing set of disciplines, rather than five separate finished games.

release.text: Tectoy released Baja for Zeebo on 31 October 2009.

overview.text: Bóia Cross sends its riders down rapids in inner tubes. Energy drinks replenish the boost, and the guide advertises special tricks. Its three courses are named Santo André, Bonito and Caverna do Diabo.

development.text: Tiago Tex Pine led design across the Extreme series. Level layouts were worked out with the 3D environment artists and QA staff.

release.text: Bóia Cross was released for Zeebo on 21 December 2009. It is also known as Zeebo Extreme Acqua Ride.

Writing in 2019, original-console owner rodrigo found Bóia Cross enjoyable in short sessions, but soon repetitive alone. His criticism was concrete: after finishing a race, there was little beyond repeating the three courses and improving records. He had not tested two-player play because he owned only one controller.

276809.deck: Downhill racing in a carrinho de rolimã.

overview.text: A carrinho de rolimã is a small soapbox cart. This racer sends four selectable characters down courses named after São Paulo, Petrópolis and Ouro Preto. Gravity carries the carts downhill; players brake, drift and use turbo.

development.text: Rolimã opened the five-game Extreme series. Tiago Tex Pine led its game and interface design, alongside production of the series.

For Tectoy Digital, the Extreme games were original productions rather than conversions. A February 2009 preview described an initial package of rolimã, inner-tube racing and aircraft races, with more disciplines planned later. The released series instead arrived as separate games.

QA analyst Suzana Bueno described a deliberate balance: the carts should feel a little beyond the driver’s control, while leaving room to become skilled. Her account also places QA within the creative work, from the engine’s creation to adjusting cameras.

Bueno singled out the Liberdade arches, Avenida Paulista’s flower beds and triangular FIESP building, a roadside cheese shop in Petrópolis, and Ouro Preto’s churches at sunset. She described these details as reflections of the people making the game.

release.text: Rolimã was released for Zeebo on 15 August 2009.

RssV’s review for Blog Zeebo Brasil, preserved by Kito Games, tested the Z-Pad version. It praised responsive braking and drifting and a stable sense of speed, while finding the computer opponents easy to beat. Three courses and the absence of a tournament or career left local two-player racing as the main reason to return. The reviewer awarded 8/10.

279380.deck: Four football challenges starring the player’s Zeeboid.

overview.text: Foot Camp separates football into penalties, free kicks, dribbling and keep-ups. The free-kick game adds wind and a defensive wall; dribbling asks players to repeat button sequences. Power-ups can turn a goalkeeper into a chicken or have aliens abduct opponents.

development.text: Tiago Tex Pine designed Foot Camp for friends playing together. Three activities use turns and score comparisons, while Goal Scoring allows direct, simultaneous competition. He led a twelve-person team and worked on the game design, interface wireframes, balancing and user testing.
The game used C++, BREW and Adreno SDKs, with an internal OpenGL ES engine developed by Tectoy Digital and Zeebo Studios.

The original plan paired a low-priced Foot Camp with a free Zeeboids application, using friends’ visits to introduce more people to the console. Pine’s work included pitching to Zeebo, documenting the design and testing its balance; the avatar system and the game were meant to reinforce each other.

release.text: Zeebo announced Foot Camp and Zeeboids together on 3 June 2010 for Brazil and Mexico. Zeebo Interactive Studios in Brazil created both. The announcement described groups of up to eight taking turns.

The Brazilian launch campaign was tied to the 2010 World Cup. GameReporter’s David de Oliveira Lemes, contacted directly by producer Tiago Tex Pine, reported a 1,490 Z-Credit introductory price while Brazil remained in the tournament, followed by 1,690 Z-Credits. 278738.deck: Four-a-side dodgeball with the Zeebo Sports cast.

overview.text: Queimada is dodgeball. Its teams have four players, and the Boomerang version uses swinging motions to throw or dodge while characters move automatically. Buttons handle passing, catching and taunting.
The Portuguese guide also advertises new character outfits to unlock.

Passing and feinting are central to attacks. In the original Boomerang version, button 1 lets a player fake a throw, while button 2 passes to a teammate. Without the ball those buttons taunt and attempt a catch; a motion upward dodges. Two camera views offer a different look at the court.

development.text: Hugo Faria produced the game. Bruno Evangelista and Tiago Monteiro Fernandes led programming, Seigi Sato led art, and Denis Koishi supplied music.

release.text: The original Boomerang Sports Queimada was released on 5 February 2010. Its Zeebo Sports relaunch added Z-Pad controls in August 2010; two-player games required matching controller types.

277534.deck: Doubles tennis with unlockable rackets and motion controls.

overview.text: Tênis plays doubles matches with characters that move automatically. With the Boomerang, the player swings to hit the ball. Winning earns points towards unusual rackets, including a guitar, broom and frying pan.

development.text: Bruno Evangelista led programming and Seigi Sato led art. The credits name Hugo Faria as producer and André Nogueira as acting producer, with further programming, art and testing recorded in a separate 2010 additional-resources section.

At SBGames 2009, Bruno Evangelista used Tênis to illustrate the studio’s progress: a contemporaneous report quotes him comparing 10,000 triangles per scene in Tênis with 6,000 in Rolimã. These were the lead programmer’s stated figures, rather than an independent benchmark.

release.text: Tênis began as a Boomerang-only game on 15 October 2009. The August 2010 Zeebo Sports edition added Z-Pad play. Existing owners could request a free upgrade, which erased their local progress.

J.Vila’s Zeebo Club review praised the eccentric cast and unlockable rackets, but noticed a slight delay between a swing and the game’s response. He found one court and no career mode restrictive; the daily online-ranking update helped sustain competition. He awarded 7.5/10. This review concerns the original Boomerang release.

overview.text: Vôlei covers serving, attacks, blocks and defensive returns. Characters move automatically, while the player times actions with the controller. One or two players choose doubles teams, and victories earn points towards costumes.
The Boomerang’s directional pad changes the camera; its buttons handle jumping and blocking.

development.text: Hugo Faria produced Vôlei. Bruno Evangelista and Tiago Monteiro Fernandes led programming; Seigi Sato led art, with Paula Carneiro Amin, Pedro Hamaya and Carina Cheng among the artists.
Its voice cast included Rafael Marques, Cacau Pastorello, Danny Caldas, Suellen Carollo and Carina Cheng, alongside Denis Koishi’s music.

release.text: Vôlei was released on 14 December 2009 as Boomerang Sports Vôlei. The August 2010 Zeebo Sports relaunch added Z-Pad controls while keeping the same game.

The later games prompted comparisons with Vôlei. In his April 2010 Queimada review, STX preferred Vôlei’s music to the newer game’s street ambience. His May Peteca review described a related motion-control approach, with the difference that a timed swing could make the Peteca player jump without an extra button press.

overview.text: Zeeboids creates 3D characters with customizable appearances. Compatible games use those characters as players, including Foot Camp and Super League.
At launch, players could synchronize their Zeeboids, skills and achievements through ZeeboNet and retrieve them on another console, such as a friend’s system.

development.text: Tiago Tex Pine led an eight-person team and handled the core product design. Nintendo’s Miis were an explicit inspiration. He worked with programmers to decide how much appearance customization the hardware could support while maintaining the frame rate.
The application used the team’s internal OpenGL ES engine with C++, BREW and Adreno SDKs.

Pine’s original intention was an avatar system native to the console, with Zeeboids initially free on the store. The characters would be reused in other games, rather than staying inside a standalone editor.

release.text: Zeebo announced Zeeboids alongside Foot Camp in June 2010. Both were developed by Zeebo Interactive Studios in Brazil.

Launch-era Brazilian reporting listed Zeeboids separately at 290 Z-Credits, alongside Foot Camp’s promotional price. That differs from the original free-distribution intention Pine recalls in his portfolio. The same report presented the avatars as a continuing part of later games in the football series.

overview.text: Dark Seal offers four heroes with different weapons: a knight, bard, magician and ninja. Alongside their ordinary attacks, spells and transformations give them other ways to fight through the monsters.

The isometric view allows movement in eight directions. Killing enemies fills a magic meter while a book cycles through available spells. Casting at the right moment transforms the character, with forms including a tornado, a Medusa head and a giant rat accompanied by smaller rats. Treasure can temporarily improve speed, strength or defence.

279889.deck: Infiltrate a missile base and assemble a weapon from six hidden parts.

overview.text: Heavy Barrel is an overhead shooter set in a nuclear missile installation seized by terrorists. Its most powerful weapon was dismantled and locked away: the player collects keys and recovers its six parts while fighting through the base. Two players can tackle the mission together.

Movement and firing direction are independent. STX described using the analog stick to move and the ZL/ZR shoulder buttons to rotate the soldier’s aim. A player has to turn the gun towards an approaching enemy rather than assuming that walking towards it will also aim the weapon.

development.text: The original Data East arcade game appeared in 1987. Its credits name Koji Akibayashi for game design and Azusa Hara and Hiroaki Yoshida for music and sound. Onan Games later handled the Zeebo port.

release.text: Heavy Barrel reached the Brazilian Zeebo catalog on 27 July 2010, published by G-Mode.

quotes.translation: English translation by the archive: “Personally, I find myself wanting to play Karnov’s more than Tekken 2.”

279200.deck: Match colored balls before the descending pile fills the playfield.

overview.text: Magical Drop III puts the player beneath a descending field of coloured balls. Pull down balls of one colour, move sideways and throw them back to complete matches. The Zeebo controls use button 1 to collect balls, button 2 to return them and button 3 to bring the ball field down.

Survival lasts as long as the player can keep up. Challenge pits a chosen character against successive opponents. Magical Journey adds a board-game route with separate challenges, items and bosses. Two players can compete directly.

development.text: Onan Games handled the Zeebo port of Data East’s puzzle game. G-Mode included it in its March 2010 announcement.
The Zeebo Data East releases used emulation.

release.text: The Brazilian Zeebo release is dated 22 April 2010.

STX’s April 2010 review awarded 8.5/10, praising the animation, presentation and responsive controls. The pace distinguished it from the more relaxed Bejeweled Twist: there was little time to plan while the balls kept descending. Repeated character voices were one of his reservations.

quotes.text: É pressão que não acaba mais!
quotes.speaker: STX
quotes.attribution: Zeebo Club review, 29 April 2010
quotes.translation: English translation by the archive: “It’s pressure that never lets up!”

276212.deck: Collect dots in isometric mazes while avoiding the ghosts.

overview.text: Pac-Mania moves PAC-MAN’s dot collecting into an isometric maze. Clear the dots to reach the next round, use power pellets to turn the tables on the ghosts, and jump over pursuers when the route is blocked. Some ghosts can jump too.

The Z-Pad’s D-pad or analog stick moves Pac-Man, while button 1 jumps. The Zeebo store description reproduced in Mig64’s review advertised 256 levels. Different ghost behaviour and changing maze layouts supply the variations as play continues.

development.text: Namco released the arcade original in 1987. Tomoyuki Shimizu designed the game, with Shimizu and Toru Iwatani credited as directors. The Zeebo release record names Namco Bandai Games as the port developer and publisher.

release.text: Pac-Mania was released for Zeebo in Brazil on 16 June 2009, distributed by Tectoy.

Mig64’s April 2010 review gave Pac-Mania 7/10. He liked the controls, clear interface and persistence of the score-chasing game, while finding its sound much less impressive. His ratings split sharply: 9 for gameplay and 4 for sound.

quotes.text: A jogabilidade é simples também, mas boa.
quotes.speaker: Mig64
quotes.attribution: Zeebo Club review, 24 April 2010
quotes.translation: English translation by the archive: “The gameplay is simple too, but good.”

278987.deck: Johnny and Tom pursue a kidnapped girlfriend with a magical yo-yo.

overview.text: Johnny and Tom set off on a treasure hunt after a kidnapping. Their weapons include a magical yo-yo, used to fight through the platform stages.

The yo-yo is only the starting weapon. Bombs, boxing gloves, ice knives, fireballs and shurikens change the available attacks. Button 1 attacks and can be held for a charged strike; button 2 jumps, while button 3 uses a weapon-specific special move.

development.text: Spin Master was among the first three Data East games announced for Zeebo in March 2010. Onan Games made the port for publisher G-Mode.
The Zeebo Data East releases used emulation.

release.text: Release records list Spinmaster in Mexico on 31 March 2010 and Brazil on 16 April.

STX found the controls responsive and the presentation stronger than Caveman Ninja’s, but considered Spin Master much easier. He completed it with a less experienced second player reaching the final boss alongside him. That cooperative play impressed him more than the short solo campaign.

quotes.text: Fecho o game dentro de 30-35 minutos.
quotes.speaker: STX
quotes.attribution: Zeebo Club review, 26 April 2010
quotes.translation: English translation by the archive: “I finish the game in 30–35 minutes.”

278988.deck: Three-a-side basketball with high jumps and exaggerated dunks.

overview.text: Street Hoop plays basketball with three-player teams. Matches emphasize quick attacks, high jumps and exaggerated slam dunks.

Two action buttons cover shooting, passing, blocking and steals. Successful baskets fill a power meter for exaggerated special shots. The Zeebo release supports two-player matches, but movement relies on the D-pad rather than the analog stick.

development.text: G-Mode’s March 2010 announcement used the name Street Slam. Onan Games ported the Data East game to Zeebo.
The Zeebo Data East releases used emulation.

release.text: The Brazilian Zeebo edition is dated 16 April 2010. The game also appears in international catalogs as Street Slam and Dunk Dream.

STX’s April 2010 review praised its pace and reported no noticeable lag. He liked the music and competitive replay value, while criticising the lack of analog support on the Z-Pad. Even though he did not usually enjoy basketball games, he kept wanting another match.

quotes.text: o game possui multiplayer. Diversão garantida!
quotes.speaker: STX
quotes.attribution: Zeebo Club review, 22 April 2010
quotes.translation: English translation by the archive: “the game has multiplayer. Guaranteed fun!”

279125.deck: Jump on burger ingredients to drop them onto the plates below.

overview.text: Peter Pepper Jr. and his twin brother Pete assemble burgers by jumping on their ingredients. Each layer drops toward a serving plate, with food enemies chasing the cooks around the platforms and ladders. Falling ingredients can crush those enemies.

The pepper shaker is the starting weapon, with other weapons and items appearing at the edge of the screen. Attacks can be directed up or down while on a ladder. Jumping, attacking and dropping burger layers have to be balanced against a constant supply of new enemies.

development.text: Data East released the arcade original in 1990. Its credits name Koji Akibayashi as game designer, Mario Watanabe and Yoshiyuki Urushibara as graphic designers, and Tatsuya Kiuchi and Tomoyoshi Sato for sound. Onan Games made the Zeebo port.
The Zeebo Data East releases used emulation.

release.text: G-Mode announced Super Burger Time for Zeebo in March 2010. The Brazilian release is dated 16 April.

STX praised its simple, responsive controls and difficult stages in April 2010. The tiny characters could be hard to distinguish, even on a large television. He separated his verdict for older and newer players—7.1/10 and 6.1/10—but his complaint about continuing a hard run was concrete:

quotes.text: Esse mereceria suporte a Save States!
quotes.speaker: STX
quotes.attribution: Zeebo Club review, 30 April 2010
quotes.translation: English translation by the archive: “This one ought to support save states!”

276731.deck: Namco’s second Iron Fist Tournament, released for Zeebo in 2009.

overview.text: Tekken 2 is a one-on-one fighting game. The Zeebo guide advertises 25 fighters and move sets from the arcade game.

Arcade play unlocks hidden fighters, Survival tests how many opponents one life bar can overcome, and Training provides room to practise combinations. Versus supports a second player. The Zeebo edition has Portuguese menu text, but no individual character ending movies.

development.text: Seiichi Ishii directed and designed the original Namco arcade game. Its credits also name Masahiro Kimoto as motion manager.
Before launch, John Rizzo said it was not a mobile conversion, but could not identify which earlier platform supplied the port.

release.text: Namco Bandai Games America published Tekken 2 for Zeebo in Brazil on 8 October 2009, with Tectoy handling distribution.

Mig64 expected little from the slow-looking trailer. After playing the released game, he described much smoother animation, responsive controls and a useful choice of D-pad or analog movement. Missing character voices and endings disappointed him. He initially undervalued its replay appeal, then revised that part after repeatedly returning to play.

Writing as an owner in 2019, Douglas Deiró also regretted the absent endings, but valued the full fighter roster and the revised character models. He considered the remaining game worth playing on the console he actually owned.

quotes.text: É meu jogo favorito do Zeebo
quotes.speaker: Mig64
quotes.attribution: Comment beneath his Zeebo Club review, 26 April 2010
quotes.translation: English translation by the archive: “It’s my favourite Zeebo game.”

quotes.text: Ah! Não tem filminho? Posso ver no Youtube
quotes.speaker: Douglas Deiró
quotes.attribution: QG Master, 6 August 2019; syndicated by Retroinvaders
quotes.translation: English translation by the archive: “Oh! No movie? I can watch it on YouTube”

280463.deck: Two cavemen clear creature-filled platform stages with clubs, fire and ice.

overview.text: A scientist named Ragor travels into the past and kidnaps Kama. Tork and Kral pursue him through 60 levels, fighting dinosaurs, bears and other creatures with clubs. Fire and ice upgrades let the cavemen trap enemies before finishing them off.
The game supports two players working together. Its Escape mode changes the objective to climbing fast enough to stay ahead of the scrolling screen.

development.text: The game first appeared publicly as Ice and Rock. In April 2010, Zeebo Club’s Saulo Albert reported that Vega Mobile had displayed prototype images of three planned Zeebo games: XGT Racer, Code Devil and Ice and Rock.

By September it had become Tork and Kral. A ZeeboBrasil report, based on contact with producer Jerome Schurch, described pre-rendered 3D graphics, 60 stages and simultaneous two-player play. The writers noted that the later images looked markedly different from the early prototype.

Schurch said the game was awaiting Zeebo’s approval and expected it within one or two weeks. The same report said Vega was working on further original prototypes and seeking investment to finish them.

release.text: The official Zeebo blog announced Tork and Kral on 16 November 2010, later than the September report’s expected window. It advertised solo or cooperative play and specified two wired controllers for two players.

credits.name: Jerome Schurch
credits.role: Producer, identified in contemporary developer report

278965.deck: Defend a toy battlefield against bombers and paratroopers.

overview.text: Toy Raid puts the player behind a cannon, defending a base from toy aircraft and parachuting soldiers. Bombs threaten the base from above; soldiers who land can attack it from inside. Power-ups add guided bullets, scatter shots and other weapons.

The Zeebo version uses the Z-Pad rather than the iPhone’s tilt control. STX reported no Boomerang support and found the cannon slow to turn; holding button 1 kept it firing. Leaving and returning preserved the current stage, but losing all lives did not give an unlimited continue.

development.text: Toy Raid was Flying Tiger’s first Zeebo project. John Brandstetter described its origins:
The Zeebo credits name Michael Fernie for programming, Jeremy Klein for art and Brian Twist for testing.

release.text: Toy Raid launched for Zeebo in March 2010. A contemporary company announcement described it as Flying Tiger’s first game for the system.

STX gave the game 5.7/10 in his May 2010 Zeebo Club review. He criticised the simple backgrounds and saturated sound effects, while finding the different weapons useful. His verdict treated it as a short-session diversion:

quotes.text: Our first game for Zeebo, Toy Raid, was ported and enhanced from the iPhone version
quotes.speaker: John Brandstetter
quotes.attribution: President of Flying Tiger Entertainment, in Zeebo’s press release, 12 April 2010

quotes.text: É um otimo passa tempo e só.
quotes.speaker: STX
quotes.attribution: Zeebo Club review, 3 May 2010
quotes.translation: English translation by the archive: “It’s a great pastime, and that’s all.”

263019.deck: Chess with animated mechanical pieces and 3D capture sequences.

overview.text: Ultimate Chess 3D plays on a conventional chessboard, then switches to animated battles when a piece captures another. Its mechanical pieces can be customized with parts bought through the game’s foundry.

Alongside local two-player chess, there are ordinary and timed games against the computer. Winning earns gears, the in-game currency spent on pieces, boards, backgrounds, tutorials and analyses of historical matches. Players can also stake their gears on a game for a larger reward.

development.text: Superscape’s game appeared on BREW phones in 2007 before reaching Zeebo in 2009. The Zeebo credit transcription names Viacheslav Dubikovsky as producer, Brian Collins as game designer and Ian Livingstone for sound and music.

In January 2009, Zeebo CEO John Rizzo said the conversion from Glu’s BREW version had taken four months. He described a proposed wireless two-player edition as manageable because only the moves needed transmitting.

release.text: Glu Mobile published the Zeebo edition in 2009.

Mig64’s April 2010 review liked the animated captures and range of unlockable material, but reported pauses before animations and very little audio. The workshop appeared to download purchases, yet no new content had arrived by his review. Players who only wanted chess could disable the combat animations.

notes.text: The wireless edition discussed before launch was a proposal, not confirmation that online play shipped.

quotes.text: Atualizações, aonde estão?
quotes.speaker: Mig64
quotes.attribution: Zeebo Club review, 27 April 2010
quotes.translation: English translation by the archive: “Updates, where are they?”

279173.deck: Five heroes fight monsters with weapons and magic.

overview.text: Wizard Fire sends five fantasy heroes through a kingdom filled with monsters, weapons, magic and treasure. It can be played alone or with a second player.

development.text: Onan Games ported Data East’s game to Zeebo. G-Mode announced it in March 2010 under the spelling Wizard of Fire.
The Zeebo Data East releases used emulation.

release.text: Wizard Fire was released for Zeebo in Brazil on 16 April 2010.

Ahtrun reviewed Wizard Fire the day after its recorded Brazilian release. He enjoyed the cooperative play and reported no lag, but the Z-Pad’s D-pad was a major obstacle. The unchanged English story also made it less accessible to the Brazilian audience the console was meant to reach.

quotes.speaker: Ahtrun

quotes.translation: English translation by the archive: “Honestly, playing without analog is extremely difficult”

platform.heading: A console with mobile roots
platform.text: Zeebo Inc. was formed by Tectoy and Qualcomm. Its console used Qualcomm mobile technology and delivered games through a built-in 3G connection instead of discs. At GDC 2009, the company presented a system intended for households in developing markets.

platform.heading: The intended audience
platform.text: In May 2009, CEO John Rizzo discussed an initial Brazilian rollout, followed by Mexico. The executives described a mix of established games and new titles suited to local audiences. Qualcomm’s Mike Yuen explained their approach to finding that content:

quotes.text: We don't just have to take everything in the Western world and force it on people in another world.
quotes.speaker: Mike Yuen, Qualcomm
quotes.attribution: Interview with Brandon Sheffield, Gamasutra, 20 May 2009

platform.heading: Why BREW was chosen
platform.text: Reinaldo Normand told UOL in 2014 that the team had considered Symbian, Java and Linux before choosing BREW. He recalled Nokia’s commitment to N-Gage, concerns about Java piracy, and the cost of adapting Linux. BREW offered an existing shop and copy-protection system. This was a commercial and distribution decision as well as a hardware choice.

platform.heading: What the production team encountered
platform.text: In the same interviews, André Penha described an operating system still carrying telephone functions that the console did not need. Stefano Arnhold recalled that hardware limitations made adapting games much more expensive than expected. Looking back, Normand regretted positioning the console against the PlayStation 2 while offering less power and fewer games.

platform.heading: A programmer’s account from 2008
platform.text: Carol Gomes wrote about Zeebo before its retail launch. During her Tectoy internship, she and colleagues had added multiplayer to an unnamed football game and a racing game. She remembered having to work through difficult source code. Her post also argued that original games and a route for independent developers would be important to the console’s future.

quotes.text: so big and absolutely uncommented
quotes.speaker: Carol Gomes
quotes.attribution: Personal development blog, 16 November 2008; describing the games’ existing source code

platform.heading: The development environment
platform.text: The May 2009 Developer Guide describes Zeebo software version 1.0 as based on Qualcomm’s BREW 4.0.2 SDK, with OpenGL ES graphics and IHID controller extensions. Its specifications list VGA television output at 640 × 480 in a 4:3 aspect ratio.

platform.heading: Tools and testing
platform.text: The guide covers memory management, controller input, 3D graphics, audio, debugging and game submission. It includes instructions for BREW AppLoader and Logger, loading builds from an SD card, and tuning television output. Developers’ individual accounts describe how they used this environment for particular games.

platform.heading: The shop closes
platform.text: In May 2011, Zeebo announced the end of its Brazilian operations and Zeebo Interactive Studios. Its statement kept the online shop open until 30 September, with reduced game prices during the remaining months. Purchased content would remain usable on the console. After that deadline, a working machine’s installed library mattered in a way it had not when owners could still buy another download.

platform.heading: The surviving collection
platform.text: OpenZeebo’s compilation notes are dated 23 October 2011. They map numeric application IDs to game and system-app names. The archive retains those IDs, the original package variants and the measured file fingerprints, alongside the game histories.

platform.heading: Documenting the people as well as the software
platform.text: Former Tectoy Digital employee Bruno de Paula later began researching the company he had worked for, interviewing former colleagues and presenting its history. Reporting from the History of Games conference in 2024, John Szczepaniak described de Paula’s account of the studio’s split into Tectoy Studios and Zeebo Interactive Studios. He also reported their discussion of enthusiasts preserving the released games and the difficulties of installing dumps on original hardware.
